Systems Programming and Machine Organization
Chapter 12: Instruction Set Architecture
Dr. Charles Dorner

1. An instruction is a state-change contract
Problem and first experiment

SAY
To understand machine code, start with what each instruction promises to change. A load changes a destination value, arithmetic changes a result and often flags, and a branch changes where execution continues. Together these updates describe architectural state, meaning the state that the instruction set exposes to software. The physical processor may use several smaller internal steps or overlap independent work. That does not make the instruction contract disappear. Our models make state changes explicit with small C++ values, but they are not x86 emulators and do not measure a real processor's cycle count.

DO
Ask learners to name one data-state change and one control-state change.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch12.json → SP12.004

------------------------------------------------------------

2. Trace a load, multiply, and store
Problem and first experiment

SAY
This small machine model has one accumulator, one memory cell, and an instruction index. Loading three leaves index one and accumulator three. Multiplying by four leaves index two and accumulator twelve. Storing that value changes the memory cell to twelve and advances the index to three. The printed trace reports these exact boundaries. Ordinary C++ statements implement the model; they are not an instruction encoding or a timing simulation. The unsigned values keep this tiny example within a clearly valid range. We use the model to separate data state from control state before inspecting the much richer x86 instruction set.

DO
Predict all three trace lines before running.

SOURCE
Lecture demonstration for content/systems-programming/ch12.json → SP12.016

------------------------------------------------------------

3. Control flow needs a work budget
Problem and first experiment

SAY
A program can stay inside its instruction array and still run forever. Our second model has two instructions, each jumping to the other. Both target indices are valid. Starting at zero, five steps visit the alternating targets and finish at one, so the output reports steps five and pc one. The halt flag remains false because no instruction requested termination. A separate execution budget stops the model. This is a controlled demonstration of a missing progress guarantee, not an intentionally hanging program. An interpreter for untrusted input needs both valid-address checks and a resource bound; either alone leaves a different failure mode open.

DO
Trace the target sequence 1, 0, 1, 0, 1.

SOURCE
Lecture demonstration for content/systems-programming/ch12.json → SP12.022

------------------------------------------------------------

4. The program counter is not a loop counter in every ISA
Problem and first experiment

SAY
The tiny model increments its program counter by one because each vector slot is one modeled instruction. Real x86-64 instructions have variable-length byte encodings, so sequential instruction addresses do not generally differ by one. If an instruction begins at hexadecimal one thousand and occupies seven bytes, the next address is one thousand seven. A RIP-relative displacement is based on that next address, not automatically the address printed at the start of the disassembly line. Keep the model's units visible. Confusing instruction indices with byte addresses creates a plausible-looking trace that reaches the wrong target.

DO
Compare three one-slot model instructions with hypothetical two-, five-, and three-byte encodings.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch12.json → SP12.010

8. Chapter 12 — Instruction Set Architecture
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
The instruction set is the boundary between software’s requested operations and a processor’s implementation. It describes registers, instructions, address calculations, and architectural effects. It does not specify that every instruction takes one cycle or that internal work occurs in source order. Reading assembly well requires keeping the architectural result separate from the microarchitectural method.

10. Machine instructions
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
A machine instruction is an encoded operation the processor recognizes. It identifies an operation and, explicitly or implicitly, its operands. Instructions can move data, perform arithmetic, change control flow, or request privileged behavior. On x86-64, instructions have variable-length encodings rather than one fixed size. The visible instruction sequence is not necessarily the processor’s internal execution sequence. A processor may decode instructions into smaller operations, overlap independent work, and speculate past branches. Architectural rules determine what results may become visible. An assembly listing is therefore a semantic description and an input to performance analysis, not a cycle-by-cycle hardware trace.

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.
Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch12.json → SP12.004, SP12.005

------------------------------------------------------------

11. Registers
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Registers are named architectural storage locations used directly by instructions. General-purpose registers hold integer values and addresses. Other register classes support vector, floating-point, control, and status operations. Keeping a value in a register can avoid a memory access, but the number and use of registers are constrained by the ISA and ABI. Architectural register names need not correspond one-to-one with fixed physical storage inside a modern processor. Register renaming can map successive architectural values to different physical registers. This helps remove false dependencies while preserving the program’s required register behavior. Source-level programmers normally need the architectural model first and the renaming model only for deeper performance work.

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.
Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

12. Memory
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Instructions access memory through effective addresses computed from available operands. A load brings a value into a register or another destination; a store writes a value to memory. Some x86 instructions combine memory access with arithmetic, but that does not eliminate the underlying data movement. A memory operand can involve address translation, cache lookup, coherence, and fault checks. Two instructions with similar arithmetic can have very different costs if one waits for a cache miss. Count memory traffic and dependencies, not just mnemonics, when estimating performance.

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.
Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch12.json → SP12.008, SP12.009

13. Program counter
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
The program counter identifies the instruction position used for control flow. On x86-64 the architectural instruction pointer is %rip . Sequential execution advances to the next instruction; branches, calls, returns, and exceptions change the flow according to their rules. For RIP-relative addressing, the displacement is interpreted relative to the next instruction’s address. This detail matters when manually calculating a target from disassembly. The value displayed beside an instruction is usually its own starting address, not necessarily the base used in that instruction’s relative-address computation.

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.
Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

14. Processor state
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Processor state includes more than general-purpose registers. It can include condition flags, vector registers, floating-point control state, stack state, privilege state, and address-translation configuration. The exact state relevant to an operation depends on the architecture and execution context. A context switch must preserve enough state for a thread to resume as though its execution had been paused. A normal function call has a narrower contract: the calling convention specifies which registers the caller or callee must preserve. Confusing a context switch with a function call leads to incorrect assumptions about who saves what.

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.
Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch12.json → SP12.012, SP12.013

15. ISA versus microarchitecture
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
The ISA specifies architectural behavior. The microarchitecture is the implementation: pipelines, execution units, caches, predictors, queues, and scheduling logic. Different processors can execute the same binary while exhibiting different latency, throughput, and energy behavior. An optimization based on a particular instruction cost may not transfer to another processor implementing the same ISA. The portable part of the reasoning is the algorithm and architectural semantics; the measured part belongs to a specific machine and workload. The Intel architecture manuals separate instruction behavior from implementation-oriented performance guidance. [ R3 ]

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.
Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

16. Tracing a tiny abstract machine
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Use a deliberately simplified machine with one accumulator, a program counter, and four instructions: load immediate, add immediate, multiply immediate, and halt. This is a teaching model, not x86 assembly. Companion listing: ch12/machine.py The trace is (1,6) , (2,10) , and (3,30) . Each pair records the next instruction index and accumulator after one operation. The halt instruction leaves the final pair unchanged. The model makes control and data state explicit, but it intentionally omits fixed-width overflow, memory, interrupts, and timing. Now imagine an implementation that computes the addition and multiplication through several internal steps. As long as the architectural result at each required boundary is preserved, those internal steps need not resemble this simple interpreter. That is the distinction between an ISA-level explanation and an implementation-level explanation.

17. Separating ISA from implementation
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Two processors can both implement x86-64 and execute the same architectural instruction stream while using different pipelines, cache sizes, branch predictors, and execution widths internally. The ISA specifies programmer-visible behavior; the microarchitecture determines how a particular implementation achieves it. Performance differences therefore do not imply different source-level semantics.

18. Updating architectural state
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
For an instruction conceptually equivalent to RAX = RAX + RBX , the visible result is a new RAX and updated condition flags according to the instruction definition. Internally the processor may rename registers and execute out of order, but retirement preserves the architectural effect as though the instruction completed in program order, subject to the machine’s defined memory model.

22. Registers are named architectural storage
Reason about the implementation

SAY
A register gives an instruction a named place to obtain or store a value. A C++ variable is a source-language object, so there is no promise that every variable receives its own register. The compiler may remove a variable, reuse a register after a value dies, or spill a value to memory. Inside a modern processor, register renaming can assign successive values of one architectural register to different physical storage. Software still observes the architectural dependency rules. Begin with those rules when reading an instruction sequence; physical renaming becomes useful later when explaining why independent work can overlap without changing the final answer.

DO
Track two successive values assigned to the same named model register.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch12.json → SP12.006

------------------------------------------------------------

23. A load has more work behind it than an addition
Reason about the implementation

SAY
Two instructions may each produce one integer result while requiring very different work. Adding two ready register values uses already-available data. Loading an integer from memory first needs an effective address and a permitted translation, and may wait for data from a cache or a lower memory level. A fault can send control to the operating system. None of this means that every load is slow; many hit in a nearby cache. It means the mnemonic count alone is a poor cost model. When investigating performance, follow data dependencies and memory traffic before assigning one equal time unit to every line of assembly.

DO
Contrast a ready register add with a load whose address depends on a previous load.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch12.json → SP12.008

------------------------------------------------------------

24. Saving a thread is broader than making a function call
Reason about the implementation

SAY
A function call and a context switch both involve continuation, but their obligations differ. A normal function interface lets certain registers be overwritten and requires others to be preserved. The caller knows that agreement. A paused thread must later resume with the state needed to continue its own computation, which can include flags, vector state, stack state, and operating-system execution context. Do not use the six integer argument registers as a complete list of processor state. This distinction matters when debugging low-level code: a routine that respects the function ABI may still be wholly inadequate as a thread-switch mechanism.

DO
List one state component beyond ordinary integer arguments.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch12.json → SP12.012

------------------------------------------------------------

25. One ISA can have many implementations
Reason about the implementation

SAY
Imagine two processors running the same binary and producing the same answers. One has more execution units and a larger cache; the other uses less power and takes longer on this workload. Both can satisfy the same instruction set architecture, or ISA. Their internal designs are their microarchitectures. An instruction substitution that helps one processor may hurt another because costs and bottlenecks differ. Our state traces establish what a calculation means, not how quickly a particular chip performs it. In maintenance work, separate the correctness argument from the measurement report so a hardware upgrade does not silently invalidate a supposed universal optimization rule.

DO
Ask what machine information belongs beside a benchmark result.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch12.json → SP12.014

26. Run the complete chapter demonstration
Code, diagrams, and debugging

SAY
An abstract machine has a program counter and one accumulator. Execute LOAD 4, ADD 3, then HALT.

LOAD 4. accumulator 4; pc 1. The operation changes architectural state: the state promised by the instruction set.

ADD 3. accumulator 7; pc 2. The next instruction sees the preceding result.

HALT at position 2. No further state change in this model. How real hardware pipelines or caches these operations is a separate implementation question.

Build the complete demonstration and compare every output character. The separate lab solution includes assertions for its named acceptance checks.

29. Trace an instruction-set model
Code, diagrams, and debugging

SAY
Trace an instruction-set model. pc++ supplies the current index and then advances pc. The first model instruction loads operands[0], so accumulator becomes 4 and pc becomes 1.

An abstract machine has a program counter and one accumulator. Execute LOAD 4, ADD 3, then HALT.

The operation changes architectural state: the state promised by the instruction set. The next instruction sees the preceding result. How real hardware pipelines or caches these operations is a separate implementation question.

pc++ supplies the current index and then advances pc. The first model instruction loads operands[0], so accumulator becomes 4 and pc becomes 1.

The next model instruction adds operands[1], making accumulator 7 and pc 2. These C++ statements model instruction effects; they do not dictate the compiler’s machine instructions.

pc selects the next modeled instruction operand and advances once per modeled step. Each access stays within operands.

This C++ program models an instruction sequence. Its C++ statements are not an encoding of any real ISA. In the extended lab: Fall through from Load into Add by omitting break. LOAD 4 then leaves 8 rather than 4 in the accumulator.

40. Chapter summary and maintenance
Recall and transfer

SAY
An enum gives each modeled operation a distinct name. A small struct now earns its place because an instruction consists of both an operation and an operand. The switch defines the instruction semantics while the vector traversal supplies the next instruction. The model is deliberately not a binary encoding or a real processor pipeline.

Choose a simpler approach when its narrower contract is enough. Use a real assembler and ISA manual when instruction encoding or exact machine effects matter.

When this system changes, retain a check that exposes the known failure: Fall through from Load into Add by omitting break. LOAD 4 then leaves 8 rather than 4 in the accumulator. End each non-returning case explicitly and test a one-instruction effect before testing a whole program.

41. Instruction completion is an observable boundary
Recall and transfer

SAY
Our model updates accumulator and index together after each operation, which makes reasoning easy. A real processor may start later independent work before earlier work has finished. It still must preserve the permitted architectural results, including the defined memory model and precise exception rules where applicable. This is why a software trace can reason about instruction effects without pretending to describe every internal queue. Avoid two extremes: assuming literal one-at-a-time hardware, or assuming out-of-order execution allows arbitrary answers. The architecture defines the permitted observations; the implementation chooses an efficient route within that contract.

DO
Separate an internal scheduling guess from a required register result.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch12.json → SP12.020

------------------------------------------------------------

42. Extend the model by stating what it omits
Recall and transfer

SAY
If you extend the model to sum one through five, first define the state needed for the counter, accumulator, branch, and halt. State which target values are legal and retain a step budget even when your intended program terminates. Then define arithmetic behavior. The chapter's simple interpreter is adequate for small chosen operands, but arbitrary signed additions can exceed the C++ int range. A robust extension must check that range or choose a documented modular type. This is how a teaching model grows responsibly: each new promise receives a rule and a test, and omitted timing or hardware details remain clearly labeled.

DO
Ask for one valid program, one invalid target, and one budget-exhaustion test.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch12.json → SP12.022
